question.text: Webber et al.'s widely-cited 2022 estimate puts breaking a Bitcoin key at 1.9 billion physical qubits. If someone quotes 1.9 billion as the cost of breaking a Bitcoin key "eventually," with no time pressure, are they using the number correctly?
options: No — 1.9 billion is specifically the cost of breaking a key inside Bitcoin's roughly ten-minute confirmation window, a much harder target than breaking it with unlimited time
Yes — the 1.9 billion figure was always defined as the cost with no time constraint at all
No — 1.9 billion has been superseded and retracted; only the 2026 half-million figure should ever be quoted
Yes, and the confirmation-window version of the attack would actually need a smaller number of qubits, not the same one
question.hint: Racing a transaction's confirmation window and having unlimited time to break the same key are two very different attacks. Which one does 1.9 billion price?

explain.g: How hard an attack is depends heavily on the deadline it has to work with. Breaking a key with no time limit at all is one problem; breaking it inside the roughly ten minutes a Bitcoin transaction has before it confirms is a much harder, faster version of the same problem. 1.9 billion prices the harder, time-pressured version — quoting it for the easier, unlimited-time version would be citing the right number for the wrong question.
explain.y: Webber, Elfving, Weidt and Hensinger, AVS Quantum Sci. 4, 013801 (2022) targets specifically the confirmation-window threat model: an attacker who must complete the break before the transaction confirms, not one with unlimited time to eventually recover a key. That deadline is what pushes the qubit requirement as high as it is — an unlimited-time break of the same key would need a smaller machine, not the same 1.9 billion.
explain.r: This is the same paper the home-collapse and bitcoin-estimate-collapse receipts draw their 2022 baseline from; the 3,800× drop those receipts describe compares this confirmation-window figure against the 2026 re-costing's own confirmation-window figure — a like-for-like comparison. Quoting 1.9 billion against a different, looser threat model breaks that comparison and states the wrong number for the question being asked.
